indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B1.1.2.3: Understand mixtures, the types, their formation, uses and ways of separating them into their components
indicator.objective: Demonstrate understanding that a mixture is two or more objects or materials put together

skills.description: State in simple words that a mixture is two or more things put together
Identify whether a given example is a mixture or a single material
Give an example of a mixture from everyday life
Recognise that when two materials are mixed, no new material is formed

misconceptions: When you mix two things, they always make a new thing.
A mixture is only when you mix the same kind of thing.
Sugar and water is not a mixture because the sugar disappears.
Any two objects placed together are a mixture.

options: Two or more things put together
hints: Think about mixing gari and sugar.
It is a combination.
questions.explanation: A mixture is formed when two or more materials are put together.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a mixture is only when things dissolve.

questions.stem: Which of these is a mixture?
hints: Which one has two things combined?
You can mix them in a bowl.
questions.explanation: Gari and sand is a mixture of two materials.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any two things placed next to each other are mixed.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of a mixture?
options: A cup of tea with sugar
hints: Think about what is in the cup.
The sugar is mixed in.
questions.explanation: A cup of tea with sugar is a mixture of tea and sugar.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think water is a mixture because it is liquid.

questions.stem: When you mix two materials together, you get a...
hints: What is the word for things put together?
It starts with M.
questions.explanation: A mixture is formed when two or more materials are combined.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think mixing creates a brand new element.

questions.stem: Is a bowl of plain rice a mixture?
options: Yes, because it has many grains
No, it is a single material
hints: What is in the bowl?
Is it only one thing?
questions.explanation: A bowl of plain rice is just one material (rice). It is not a mixture.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think many grains of the same thing make a mixture.

questions.stem: Which of these is a mixture?
hints: Which one has two different things?
They are both powders.
questions.explanation: Milo and milk powder mixed together is a mixture.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think any powder is a mixture.

questions.stem: Kofi puts stones and sand in a bucket. Is this a mixture?
options: Yes, because there are two materials
No, because they are both hard
No, because they are from the ground
hints: How many different things are in the bucket?
Are they combined?
questions.explanation: Stones and sand is a mixture of two different materials.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think things must dissolve to be a mixture.

questions.stem: When you mix sugar and water, do you make a new material?
options: No, the sugar and water are still there
hints: Can you taste the sugar?
The sugar is still there, just dissolved.
questions.explanation: Mixing sugar and water forms a mixture, but no new material is made. The sugar and water are still there.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the sugar disappears completely and a new liquid is formed.

questions.stem: Give an example of a mixture you can make in the kitchen.
hints: Think about mixing drinks.
What do you put in tea?
questions.explanation: Mixing milo and milk, or sugar and water, creates a mixture.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name a single food item like 'rice'.

questions.stem: What is formed when you put two or more things together?
hints: It starts with M.
Think of gari and sand.
questions.explanation: A mixture is formed when two or more things are put together.
questions.misconception: Pupils may answer with a specific object name instead of the concept.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a mixture?
options: A bowl of gari and beans
A cup of tea with milk
A mix of sand and stones
hints: Which one is only one thing?
Is there anything else in the water?
questions.explanation: A glass of pure water is a single material. The others are mixtures of different materials.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think liquids are always mixtures.

questions.stem: Ama mixes sand and iron filings. What is true about the mixture?
options: The sand and iron are still separate materials
hints: Can you still see the sand?
Can you still see the iron?
questions.explanation: In a mixture, the original materials are still there. No new material is formed.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think mixing always creates a completely new substance.

questions.stem: Which of these is a mixture of a solid and a liquid?
hints: One is solid, one is liquid.
Think about a sandy beach.
questions.explanation: Sand (solid) and water (liquid) form a mixture.
questions.misconception: Pupils may struggle to identify the states of matter in a mixture.

questions.stem: You mix gari and sugar. Explain why no new material is formed.

criteria.description: States that the gari and sugar are still there
States that it is only a combination, not a new substance

hints: Can you still taste the gari?
Can you still taste the sugar?
questions.explanation: The gari and sugar are just mixed together. They keep their own properties, so no new material is formed.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes a mixture?
options: Two or more materials combined without forming a new material
hints: Are the original materials still there?
No new thing is formed.
questions.explanation: A mixture is formed when two or more materials are combined, and the original materials keep their own properties.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think a mixture is always a new substance.

questions.stem: Kwame mixes oil and water in a bottle. What type of mixture is this?
hints: What state is oil?
What state is water?
questions.explanation: Oil and water are both liquids, so it is a liquid-liquid mixture.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think oil is a solid because it is thick.

questions.stem: Write down two different mixtures you can find in your home.

criteria.description: Gives one correct example of a mixture
Gives a second correct example of a mixture

hints: Think about food or drinks.
Is there a mix of things?
questions.explanation: Examples include tea with sugar, gari and beans, or sand and stones.

questions.stem: A student claims: 'When I mix sand and water, the sand turns into water.' Why is this FALSE?
options: Because sand is a solid and cannot turn into water
Because the sand is still in the water, just settled at the bottom
Because sand is not a material
hints: What happens if you leave the mixture to stand?
Does the sand disappear?
questions.explanation: The sand does not turn into water. It is a mixture, and the sand sinks to the bottom. Both materials are still there.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think that because the sand is covered by water, it has changed into a new material.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a mixture?
options: A bucket of sand and stones
A cup of tea with sugar
A bowl of gari and milk
hints: Which one is only one material?
It is a solid metal.
questions.explanation: A bar of pure gold is a single material, not a mixture.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think all solid objects are mixtures.
